title: Shaheedi Jor Mela
hook: in December Sikhs gather at Fatehgarh Sahib to remember the younger Sahibzade

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maghi, and the Forty Liberated who left and came back. Your line was come back, anyway. Today, a quieter gathering.

The last week of December. Much of the world is between holidays, but the roads around a Punjab town called Fatehgarh Sahib fill with people. Huge crowds come, on foot, in buses, on tractor trolleys carrying half a village. It isn't a celebration. Nobody's dressed for a party, there are no fireworks, and the mood is quiet, almost hushed. They've come to remember two little boys and their grandmother.
screen: `A TOWN FULL OF PEOPLE IN DECEMBER.` → `NOT A CELEBRATION.` → `TWO BOYS AND THEIR GRANDMOTHER.`

segments.voice: The gathering is the Shaheedi Jor Mela. Shaheedi means of the martyrs; jor mela is a gathering, a coming together. On day ninety you heard what it remembers. Tradition says the Guru's mother, Mata Gujri, and his two youngest sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, were handed over to the governor of Sirhind and held in a cold tower. The boys refused to give up their faith and were bricked into a wall and put to death, and their grandmother died in the tower. Today is about the place, and the days. The town is now called Fatehgarh Sahib, after the younger boy. Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib stands where tradition places the wall. Close by, Gurdwara Thanda Burj keeps the memory of the cold tower. A little way off is Gurdwara Jyoti Sarup, on ground that a merchant named Todar Mal, tradition says, bought for their cremation by covering it with gold coins. The mela moves between these places over several days at the end of December: unbroken readings, kirtan in tents, langar along the roads, and a long procession. Far from Fatehgarh, some families keep the whole week in mourning at home: no parties, no sweets, a mattress on the floor instead of a bed. One more name is honored in these days: Malerkotla, whose Nawab, Sher Muhammad Khan, protested in open court that children must not be punished. People sometimes say the boys were too young to understand what they were choosing. Sikhs remember it the other way: small, and yet they would not bend.
screen: `SHAHEEDI — OF THE MARTYRS.` · `THE STORY, FROM DAY NINETY.` · `THE WALL, THE TOWER, THE GOLD.` · `A WEEK ON THE FLOOR.` · then, large: `THE YOUNGER SAHIBZADE.`

segments.voice: Sit still and think of the two boys and their grandmother; you don't need to picture the wall, just them together, her hand resting on each small head. Then let the circle widen to children anywhere who are carrying things too heavy for them. If you pray, hold them all in Waheguru; if you don't, simply keep them company in the silence, the way you'd sit beside someone who is grieving.
Shaheed. Martyr: the word behind the Shaheedi Jor Mela, the gathering at Fatehgarh Sahib each December to remember the younger Sahibzade and Mata Gujri.
Your line: small, and unbending. The week behind you held an unbroken reading, a Guru's birthday, cool water, lamps for the freed, strength in joy, and coming back. Until tomorrow.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the martyrs' gathering. shaheed comes into Punjabi from Arabic, through Persian.

trapdoor: what it means: a gathering in mourning, remembering the younger Sahibzade and Mata Gujri at Sirhind.
what a scholar hears: the town was renamed Fatehgarh for Fateh Singh; Sikhs still honor Malerkotla for its Nawab's protest.
